    - Premium/high-power: Anker 737/PowerCore III 24k PD if you need multi-device fast charging.
  - Look for: USB-C PD output (18–30W+ for faster charging), pass-through charging (can charge bank and phone simultaneously), actual usable capacity vs mAh, and strong magnet alignment if MagSafe.

Important features & certifications to check

Quick fixes you can do right now
- Turn on Low Power / Battery Saver mode.
- Reduce screen brightness and set a short screen timeout (15–30s).
- Turn off Bluetooth/Wi‑Fi/Location when you don’t need them.
- Restart the phone (kills rogue apps).
- Check Settings → Battery (or Battery Usage) and see which apps use the most power; force‑stop or uninstall any surprise offenders.

Daily habits and settings to save battery
- Screen: lower brightness, enable auto/dynamic brightness, use Dark Mode if your screen is OLED.
- Timeout & refresh: shorten screen timeout and reduce refresh rate (60Hz if possible).
- Background activity: restrict background data and background activity for heavy apps (social media, streaming).
- Notifications & widgets: turn off push notifications you don’t need and remove live widgets or live wallpapers.
- Location & sync: set location to “Only while using the app” and reduce email/calendar sync frequency.
- Connectivity: use Wi‑Fi instead of cellular when possible; if you’re in poor signal areas, enable Airplane mode or turn off cellular to avoid constant searching.
- Power modes: enable adaptive battery / app standby and use battery saver when you expect long days away from a charger.

App & system maintenance
- Update apps and the OS (bug fixes often fix battery drains).
- Boot into Safe Mode (Android) to check whether a third‑party app is to blame.
- Clear cache or reinstall misbehaving apps.
- As a last resort, a factory reset can eliminate software causes.

Charging and battery health
- Use manufacturer‑approved chargers/cables. Wired charging is usually more efficient than wireless.
- Avoid charging in very hot conditions and remove thick cases if the phone gets hot while charging.
- For lithium‑ion health: avoid frequent full 0→100 or 100→0 cycles. Keeping the battery roughly between 20–80% typically extends long‑term life. Modern phones do offer optimized charging if you keep them on the charger overnight.
- If battery health (iPhone: Settings → Battery → Battery Health; Android: varies by vendor) is well below ~80%, you may need a battery replacement.

Travel / on‑the‑go tips (you mentioned a power bank)
- Carry a charged power bank and a short cable; wired charging charges faster and wastes less energy than wireless pads.
- Charge the power bank before travel; pick a power bank with at least 1–1.5× your phone’s battery capacity for a full recharge or two partial charges.
- Use low‑power mode while traveling to stretch battery between charges.

When to seek service
- If battery drains extremely fast even in Safe Mode or the phone shuts down unexpectedly at high battery percentages, contact support or get the battery checked/replaced.

Totally normal to feel nervous — Tokyo’s public transport is fast and efficient, and with a few simple rules and tools you’ll get around comfortably. Here are practical, calming tips (tailored since I know you have a Suica and are staying near Park Hyatt/Shinjuku):

Quick reassurance
- Tokyo is very safe, trains run on time, and station staff are used to helping visitors. English signs are common in big stations (like Shinjuku) and staff can usually point you the right way.

Before you go
- Make sure your phone has data (SIM or pocket Wi‑Fi) so Google Maps or a transit app can guide you in real time.
- Save your hotel address in Japanese on your phone (I can write that for you) and pin it in Maps for “home” directions.
- Keep your Suica topped up (cash at any convenience store or ticket machine) — it’s the easiest way to ride trains, subways and buses.

Using Suica and ticket machines
- Tap your Suica on the gate reader when entering and tap again when leaving. If the gate beeps, follow the display or ask staff — they’re helpful.
- Ticket machines have an English option; enter destination or fare and pay by cash or card.
- You can use Suica for small purchases at convenience stores, vending machines, and some taxis.

Navigation apps
- Google Maps is usually reliable for Tokyo (shows platforms, exits, and travel times). Alternatives: Navitime / Japan Transit Planner (Jorudan) / Tokyo Subway Navigation app for detailed subway info.
- Check platforms and exit numbers before leaving the platform; major stations have many exits and the “closest exit” matters.

Station and train etiquette
- Queue on the platform in the marked lines and board in order. Trains are quiet — keep voice and phone calls to a minimum.
- Stand on the left side of escalators in Tokyo (so people can walk on the right).
- Move toward the center of the car so others can get on at the next stop.
- Respect priority seats for elderly, disabled, pregnant, or people with small children.

Avoiding crowds and stressful times
- Avoid rush hours if possible: roughly 7:30–9:30 and 17:00–19:00 — trains get extremely crowded then.
- Many lines have women-only cars in the morning; they’re marked on the platform.

Transfers & big stations
- Give yourself extra transfer time at big stations (Shinjuku, Tokyo Station). Follow station maps and overhead signs to the correct line and exit.
- If you have luggage, use elevators/escalators at stations marked for accessibility. Coin lockers are available but can be full at peak tourist spots.

Taxis and walking
- Taxis are safe and convenient for short trips at night or when you have a lot of luggage; have your hotel name/address in Japanese to show the driver.
- Walking is pleasant in many neighborhoods (Shinjuku, Shibuya, Ginza) — comfortable shoes help.

Practical extras
- Carry a bit of cash — some smaller shops don’t take cards.
- Bring a portable charger — navigation uses battery quickly.
- Know emergency numbers: 110 (police), 119 (fire/ambulance).

  - SMS codes: one-time codes sent by text message. Widely used but vulnerable to SIM swap and interception — not the strongest choice.

  - Fingerprint, facial recognition, or other biometric checks (used on-device or as part of a second factor). Convenient, often used together with device possession.

Short answer: yes — there are several common reasons your bike (and you) will perform better in a Sunday group ride. The biggest are aerodynamic gains from drafting and steadier, faster pacing caused by the group — plus a mix of environmental, mechanical and psychological factors.

Why it feels/works better
- Drafting/pack effect: riding in a group cuts wind resistance a lot. In close formation you can save 20–30% (varies with position and spacing) of the power needed to hold a given speed. That makes the bike feel “faster” with less effort.  
- Steady pace and fewer stops: group rides typically have long, consistent pulls and fewer stop/start efforts than solo rides, so your speed is higher for the same or even lower power bursts.  
- Motivation and perceived effort: social pressure and adrenaline usually make you push harder, hold higher speeds, and tolerate harder efforts. Perceived effort often drops when you’re chatting or focused on the group.  
- Route/line choice: groups often choose smoother roads, better lines through corners, and fewer traffic interruptions.  
- Wind and weather: tailwinds or a more favorable wind direction during the ride can make the ride noticeably faster.  
- Recent maintenance/setup: you mentioned replacing your chain/cassette earlier this month — a new drivetrain reduces friction and can improve shifting and efficiency. If you pumped tires to a better pressure, lubed the chain, or had brakes free up before Sunday rides, that helps too.  
- Recovery and fueling: you might be more rested before a weekend ride or eat differently for group rides (carbs, coffee), which improves performance.

How to check which factors are in play (use your Garmin)
- If you have a power meter: compare average power or normalized power (NP) on a similar route. If speed is higher while power is lower, drafting/aero advantages are the cause. If power is higher, you’re simply riding harder in the group.  
- If no power meter: compare average heart rate and speed. Higher speed at the same or lower HR suggests drafting/aero benefit; higher HR and higher speed means you’re working harder. Check cadence too.  
- Compare ride segments: use the same Strava segment or route and compare moving time, average speed, elevation, and wind conditions.  
- Look at wind data and temperature for those rides — a tailwind can explain a big difference.

Small checks to keep performance consistent
- Keep chain/cassette and drivetrain clean and lubed.  
- Check tire pressure (and same tyre pressure for solo vs group), brake rub, wheel true, correct headset alignment.  
- Practice paceline/drafting technique to stay safe and get the most benefit.  
- If you want to replicate the group benefit solo, try doing structured intervals (e.g., tempo/threshold) or ride with a virtual paceline on a trainer.

If your current external-drive backup is working and you’re not in a rush, it’s fine to wait while you research models, shop deals, or save for a better spec.

Things to consider to help decide

- Need & urgency
  - Buy now if: you want automated, continuous backups from multiple devices, local/private storage for photos/media, or features like media streaming, home surveillance, or remote access.
  - Wait if: your data is currently backed up and accessible, your needs are experimental, or you want time to compare models/price drops.

- Budget & total cost
  - NAS enclosure + one or more drives. Drives often cost more than the NAS. Include UPS/power and potential 10GbE or NVMe costs if you want speed.
  - Consider refurbished models to save money.

- Futureproofing & features
  - Think about bay count (2-bay is simpler/cheaper; 4-bay gives more capacity/RAID flexibility).
  - Look for encryption, snapshot support, user/permission controls, and easy backup clients (Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS).
  - If you’ll stream 4K or use many apps, pick a stronger CPU and more RAM.

- Security & backup strategy
  - NAS adds convenience but is not a single backup — keep at least one off-site or external copy (cloud or removable drive).
  - Ensure the model supports encrypted volumes, account/permission controls, automatic updates, and (preferably) snapshot/replication.

- Timing vs product cycles and deals
  - There’s always a slightly newer model around the corner. Don’t delay indefinitely waiting for the “next” model.
  - If a big sale (Black Friday, Amazon Prime Day) or a rumored refresh is imminent, waiting could save money.

- Drives: buy NAS-rated drives (WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf). Don’t use consumer desktop drives for heavy always-on use.
- CPU/RAM: modest CPU + 2–4 GB RAM for backups and streaming; more for virtualization or heavy apps.
- Network: at least 1GbE; consider 2.5/10GbE if you need much higher throughput.
- Software/security: encryption, snapshot, remote access with 2FA, automatic updates.
- Backup plan: maintain a secondary backup (external drive or cloud).

2) Lemon-Ginger (bright, springy — low sugar)
- Ingredients: 1 cup unsweetened almond milk or oat milk, 1 tsp lemon zest, 1/2 tsp grated fresh ginger (or 1/4 tsp ground ginger), 1/2 tsp vanilla extract, 1–2 tsp honey or monk fruit syrup (adjust).
- Method: Warm the milk slightly, whisk or blend with ginger and zest to infuse (~5–10 min), strain if you prefer no bits. Add vanilla and sweetener to taste.
- Tip: For stronger flavor make a small ginger-lemon syrup (simmer equal parts water + 1–2 tsp sweetener with ginger + zest 5 min) and add 1–2 tsp to each cup.

3) Cinnamon-Vanilla Oat (satisfies 3–4pm sweet cravings)
- Ingredients: 1 cup unsweetened oat milk, 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon, 1 tsp vanilla, 1–2 tsp maple syrup or a dash of liquid stevia.
- Method: Whisk or blend until combined. Warm a bit for more aromatic cinnamon.

4) Mocha (chocolate-coffee boost, low added sugar)
- Ingredients: 1 cup unsweetened almond milk, 1 tsp unsweetened cocoa powder, 1/2 tsp instant espresso or strong brewed espresso concentrate, 1 tsp vanilla, sweeten lightly to taste.
- Method: Whisk cocoa into a little warm milk first to avoid clumps, then combine and blend.

5) Coconut-Cardamom (spring/flower-y, low sugar)

Quick priorities
- Playability first: neck shape, fretboard radius, string action, and how it feels in your hands matter more than looks.
- Sound second: make sure it gives the tones you want (both unplugged feel and through an amp).
- Practical: weight, balance, hardware reliability, and warranty/return policy.

What to check and how to test
- Neck & feel
  - Hold the guitar in playing position. Does the neck profile feel comfortable for your fretting hand?
  - Play all along the neck: open chords, barre chords, single-note runs. Make sure it’s comfortable in positions you use most.
- Action & frets
  - Check string action (distance to frets). Too high = hard to play; too low = buzz. Play every string at every fret to detect buzz.
  - Test bends and vibrato—no dead spots. Look at fret wear and sharp fret ends on used guitars.
- Intonation & tuning stability
  - Tune up, play a 12th-fret harmonic and compare to the fretted 12th-fret note. They should match.
  - Bend a string and see if it goes out of tune (checks nut and tuners).
- Electronics & hardware
  - Plug into an amp and try every pickup position and knob/switch. Listen for crackling/pots noise.
  - Tap the pickups with a screwdriver — they should respond evenly.
  - Check tuners, bridge, nut, and trem/locking systems for solid feel and no loose parts.
- Tone testing
  - Use the same amp and settings for every guitar so you’re comparing fairly.
  - Play styles you’ll actually use: rhythm parts, single-note lines, heavy gain and clean tones.
  - If you like fingerstyle/“acoustic-like” picking (like you mentioned Blackbird), test for clarity — humbuckers can be thicker, coil-splitting or P90s give more definition.
- Weight & balance
  - Especially with Les Pauls: they can be quite heavy. Make sure it’s comfortable standing and sitting.
- Finish & build quality
  - Inspect binding, finish flaws, neck joint, and hardware mounting.
- Documentation & return
  - Ask about warranty, return policy, and whether the guitar has any service history (for used).

Extra tips (new vs used)
- For used guitars: check for repairs, refrets, replaced necks, cracked headstocks, neck resets, and bridge repairs. Ask about original parts.
- Ask to see serial number; some quick web checks tell model/year.
- Negotiate: stores often have room on price, especially used or floor models.

What to ask the salesperson
- Has this had any setup or repairs?
- What’s the warranty/return window?
- Can you take it to a quieter area or use the same amp/preset across guitars?
- Any modded parts (pickups, nut, tuners)?

Great — here are focused, practical tips and fixes that should help you get consistently better slow-cooker results, plus a couple of gluten‑free/plant-based recipe ideas (since I remember you’ve been trying plant-based and gluten‑free options).

Top-level rules
- Less liquid than stovetop: slow cookers trap steam, so you usually need less liquid than a pot. Add only enough to barely cover ingredients unless you want a soup.
- Don’t lift the lid: every time you lift it you lose heat — about 15–20 minutes of cooking time per lift.
- Cut pieces uniform: same-size chunks cook evenly. For quick cooks, cut smaller; for long cooks, slightly larger chunks hold up better.
- Layer smart: dense root vegetables (potatoes, carrots, beets) go on the bottom, closest to the heat. Softer veggies (zucchini, peppers, mushrooms) and delicate greens go on top and/or added late.
- Sear meat first for flavor: optional for speed, but browning adds a lot of depth.
- Use dried herbs/spices at the start, fresh herbs at the end: dried needs time to bloom; fresh wilts and loses brightness if cooked too long.
- Salt later: adding salt early can draw out moisture and change texture — especially for beans, tofu, and vegetables. Add final seasoning in the last 30–60 minutes.
- Avoid thickening too early: starches and thickeners (cornstarch, arrowroot, tapioca) weaken with long heat. Use a slurry at the end and cook uncovered on high for 15–30 minutes to thicken.

Timing and temp cheatsheet
- Typical conversion: High ≈ 3–4 hours, Low ≈ 6–8 hours (varies by slow cooker and volume).
- Slow-cooker temps: Low is roughly ~180–200°F (82–93°C), High ~250–300°F (121–149°C). Use a probe thermometer if unsure.
- Beans and legumes: split lentils cook in 2–3 hours on high / 4–6 on low. Whole dried beans take longer and vary by type — red kidney beans require special caution (see below).

Important safety and bean notes
- Kidney beans: raw/undercooked red kidney beans contain a toxin (phytohaemagglutinin). Always soak AND boil kidney beans in a pot for at least 10 minutes before adding them to the slow cooker.
- Other dried beans: soak (or quick-soak) and give sufficient time. Or use canned beans and add in the last 30–60 minutes to avoid them going mushy.
- Food safety: make sure meats reach safe internal temps. If you’re unsure, use a thermometer.

Vegetarian/vegan-specific tips
- Use hearty legumes/whole grains for substance: lentils, chickpeas, black beans, barley (gluten-containing, so skip if gluten-free), quinoa (best cooked separately), buckwheat.
- Tofu/tempeh: add in the last 30–60 minutes for firmer texture; marinate or sear for flavor beforehand.
- Coconut milk and dairy: add cream, coconut milk, yogurt or cream cheese in the last 30–60 minutes to prevent separation.
- Texture control: canned beans, quick-cooking lentils, and chopped greens stirred in for the last 20–30 minutes prevent mushiness.

Thickening and finishing
- Cornstarch or arrowroot slurry: mix 1–2 tsp per cup of liquid with cold water, stir into the pot at the end and cook on high without lid until thickened.
- Reduction: remove lid and cook on high for 20–30 minutes to reduce and concentrate.
- Blend for body: use an immersion blender to puree part of the stew/chili for a creamier texture.

Yogurt (slow-cooker + cashew) reminders (you asked about this before)
- For dairy yogurt: heat milk to ~180°F to change proteins, cool to ~110°F, stir in starter, incubate 6–8+ hours. Thermometer makes this far more reliable than timing based on room temp.
- Cashew yogurt: soak cashews 4+ hours or overnight, blend until silky with water and a thickener (1–2 tbsp tapioca or cornstarch mixed in works), heat briefly to activate thickeners, cool to ~110°F, add starter/cultures and incubate. Strain if you want thicker Greek-style. A nut milk bag or fine mesh is fine; cheesecloth can lose more solids.

Common mistakes people make
- Too much liquid
- Adding delicate veg too early
